nodes.title: IP routing: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Routing is how packets find their way through a multi-network internet. Every router runs a forwarding table; routing protocols (OSPF, EIGRP, BGP) are the mechanisms by which routers exchange information and build that table.

flashcards.back: When multiple routes match a destination, the router picks the one with the most-specific (longest) prefix. So `10.0.0.0/24` beats `10.0.0.0/16` for a packet to `10.0.0.5`. This is how more-specific routes can override defaults.

It matches every destination, so it's used only when no more-specific route exists. Typically points to the internet gateway. On a stub network, the default route is often the ONLY route — everything not local goes 'up' to a smarter router.

flashcards.front: Static vs dynamic routing — when do you use each?
flashcards.back: Static routes are hand-configured, easy to understand, perfect for small or stub networks. Dynamic routing (OSPF, BGP, EIGRP) auto-discovers topology, reacts to link failures, scales to thousands of routers. Use dynamic the moment the topology is non-trivial or expected to change.

When the same destination is learned from multiple sources (static + OSPF + BGP), the router prefers the one with the lowest administrative distance. Defaults (Cisco): connected=0, static=1, EIGRP=90, OSPF=110, BGP=200. It's the tie-breaker before the routing-protocol metric.

pairs.left: An MPLS SP wants to route GOLD-tier customer traffic along a specific path satis
An OSPF ABR sits between Area 0 and a non-backbone area. It learns Type 1/2 LSAs
An OSPF design has a non-backbone Area 5 attached only to Area 2 (no direct Area
An MPLS-enabled core has hundreds of LSRs forwarding packets by label-swapping.

nodes.title: Automation and IaC: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Infrastructure as Code (IaC) means defining your servers, networks, databases in version-controlled config files instead of clicking around a console. Pipelines automate the apply step. The combination is what makes cloud reproducible.

flashcards.front: What is the value of declarative IaC?
flashcards.back: You describe the desired state ('I want 3 EC2 instances in this VPC'), the tool figures out how to get there. Reruns are idempotent — applying the same code twice doesn't double anything. State drift (someone clicked in the console) is detected on the next plan/diff.

flashcards.front: Terraform vs CloudFormation vs Bicep — what's different?
flashcards.back: Terraform: cloud-agnostic, HCL syntax, plan/apply workflow, huge ecosystem. CloudFormation: AWS-only, YAML/JSON, native rollback. Bicep: Azure-only, cleaner DSL on top of ARM. Pick the cloud-native tool if you're single-cloud; Terraform if multi-cloud or your team prefers HCL.

flashcards.front: What is a CI/CD pipeline for infrastructure?
flashcards.back: Same as for app code: commit → run linter (tflint) → plan / diff → require approval → apply. Production typically has a manual approval gate; lower environments auto-apply. Plan output is reviewed in the PR so a destructive change is caught before merge.

flashcards.front: Why is mutable infrastructure considered an anti-pattern?
flashcards.back: Mutable: SSH in, run apt-get, edit configs, server drifts from its template. Two 'identical' servers slowly diverge → snowflakes → 'works on this instance only' bugs. Immutable: bake a fresh AMI / image, replace the running instance, the old one is destroyed. Painful upfront, trivial to roll back, no drift.

questions.q: Cisco's central INTENT-BASED NETWORKING controller for ENTERPRISE network management. Provides: Design (templates), Provisioning (push to onboarded devices), Assurance (ML-based health analytics), Policy (group-based segmentation via SGTs). Renamed Catalyst Center in 2024. Which product?
choices: The APIC controller that manages an ACI data-centre fabric
Cisco DNA Center (now Catalyst Center): intent-based mgmt
questions.explanation: DNA Center automates campus network lifecycle: design (IP addressing, VLANs), policy (micro-segmentation via SGTs), provision (zero-touch deployment), assurance (AI-driven troubleshooting using network telemetry).

questions.q: Cisco NSO is a MULTI-VENDOR orchestration platform with: YANG service models, NEDs (Network Element Drivers) that translate service models to per-device configs, atomic service commits across many devices, network-wide rollback, REST + CLI + Python APIs. Which describes NSO?
choices: A hardware spine switch used in ACI fabrics
A flow collector for security analytics
questions.explanation: NSO uses service-to-device abstraction with NEDs (Network Element Drivers) for each vendor. Service templates generate device-specific configs. Transactional commits ensure all-or-nothing configuration changes.

questions.q: Network automation needs VENDOR-NEUTRAL DATA MODELS describing device configuration + state. The IETF picked a DOMAIN-SPECIFIC modelling language similar to XML Schema but human-readable. Models are used by NETCONF / RESTCONF / gNMI as the payload schema. Which language?
choices: A Python automation library for SSH access
A transport protocol running over TCP 830
A CLI templating tool for IOS configuration
questions.explanation: YANG models define what can be configured/read on a device. Example: ietf-interfaces YANG model describes interface config. Tools: pyang (validator), netmiko (CLI), ncclient (NETCONF). Cisco IOS-XE supports YANG natively. a data modeling language (RFC 6020) that defines the structure and semantics of network device configuration and state data, used with NETCONF and RESTCONF protocols.

questions.q: Cisco's older SDN controller (APIC-EM) was deprecated in 2019. Its successor (now renamed Catalyst Center) extends to Intent-Based Networking: device design + provisioning + ML-driven assurance + group-based policy. Which mapping?
choices: They are the same product with a new name only
APIC-EM is the data-centre ACI controller
DNA Center was deprecated in favour of APIC-EM
questions.explanation: APIC-EM (Application Policy Infrastructure Controller - Enterprise Module) was Cisco's first campus SDN controller. DNA Center supersedes it with: SD-Access fabric management, Assurance analytics, automation at scale.

questions.q: An automation team replaces CLI/screen-scraping with a STANDARDISED programmatic config protocol. Encodings: XML; transport: SSH (TCP 830); operations: `get-config`, `edit-config`, `commit`; supports candidate datastore + atomic commits + locks. Defined by RFC 6241. Which protocol?
choices: A JSON-over-HTTP API defined by RESTCONF
questions.explanation: NETCONF operations: <get>, <get-config>, <edit-config>, <commit>, <lock>. Uses YANG models to define data structure. Candidate datastore: edit, validate, then commit atomically. 'ncclient' is the Python library.

questions.q: A developer writing YANG-based automation for Cisco devices needs to: (a) BROWSE available YANG modules per platform, (b) GENERATE NETCONF / RESTCONF payloads from YANG, (c) TEST RPCs against a live device. Cisco ships a developer-tool web app for exactly this. Which?
questions.explanation: YANG Suite (github.com/CiscoDevNet/yangsuite): web UI to explore IOS-XE/IOS-XR YANG models, build RPC calls, test NETCONF sessions. Essential for network automation development and CCNP DevNet certification.

nodes.title: Security fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Security is about layering defenses so no single failure compromises a system. Most exams test the same core ideas: least privilege, defense in depth, the CIA triad, and the shared-responsibility line between you and your cloud provider.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality (only the right people see the data), Integrity (data isn't tampered with), Availability (the system is reachable when needed). Every security control maps to at least one of these three pillars.
Grant each identity (user, role, service account) the minimum permissions needed to do its job — no more. The opposite is wildcard access, which makes a single credential leak catastrophic.
Stack multiple, independent controls so an attacker has to defeat all of them. Example: WAF in front of an app, network ACL on the subnet, IAM on the workload, encryption at rest in the database.

flashcards.front: Shared responsibility model — who does what?
flashcards.back: The cloud provider secures the cloud (physical hardware, hypervisor, region facilities). You secure what's IN the cloud (your data, IAM config, OS patching on EC2, application code). The exact line shifts by service: serverless is more on the provider, IaaS is more on you.

questions.q: Cisco TrustSec assigns a 16-bit GROUP TAG to each authenticated endpoint at the point of authentication (via ISE). The tag propagates with the packet inline (Cisco metadata header) or via SXP (peer-to-peer). Policy enforcement compares src + dst tags at the egress device against a permissions matrix. What is this architecture?
questions.explanation: TrustSec assigns SGTs via 802.1X/ISE authentication. SGTs are carried in Ethernet headers (CMD tag) or VXLAN headers across the fabric. Policies (SGACLs) defined in ISE are enforced at fabric edges.

questions.q: Cisco's enterprise NAC platform provides: 802.1X auth + EAP, MAB (MAC Auth Bypass for non-auth-capable devices), device profiling (DHCP fingerprints + active probes), posture assessment (AV up to date? Patches?), and TrustSec policy push (SGT assignment). Which product?
choices: A VPN concentrator that terminates IPsec tunnels
A NetFlow analytics and anomaly-detection platform
questions.explanation: ISE: RADIUS/TACACS+ server + NAC + policy engine. Authenticates users/devices (Active Directory, certificates), profiles device type, checks posture (antivirus, patch level), assigns SGTs and VLANs dynamically.

questions.q: Branch users on roaming laptops need protection from malicious domains BEFORE the TCP connection is established. A cloud DNS resolver blocks lookups for known-bad domains, malware C2, phishing sites — at the DNS layer. Which Cisco product?
questions.explanation: Umbrella uses Cisco Talos intelligence to block malicious domains via DNS. All DNS queries routed through Umbrella resolvers. Provides: web filtering, malware blocking, DNS-layer security, and cloud-delivered CASB/SIG capabilities.

questions.q: A SecOps team wants behavioural anomaly detection across the network — insider threat, C2, data exfiltration patterns — by analysing NetFlow / IPFIX records over time. The platform applies ML / behavioural baselines to flag anomalies. Which Cisco product?
choices: A stateful firewall that blocks flows inline
A packet-capture appliance that stores full payloads
Cisco Stealthwatch: ML analytics over NetFlow
questions.explanation: Stealthwatch correlates flow data from routers, switches, firewalls. Detects: slow data exfiltration (beaconing), ransomware spread, compromised hosts (C2 communication), DDoS, policy violations. No agents required.

questions.q: Encrypted traffic can't be content-inspected without DECRYPTION (which is expensive + ethically contentious). Cisco's solution analyses METADATA — packet size patterns, TLS fingerprints (JA3), inter-packet timing, sequence of packet lengths — to detect malware C2 in TLS without decrypting. Which technology?
choices: A TLS decryption proxy that inspects payloads
A QoS classifier for encrypted video
questions.explanation: ETA uses machine learning to build a fingerprint of encrypted flows. Malware (even in HTTPS/TLS) has different traffic patterns than legitimate apps. Avoids privacy concerns of decryption while still detecting threats.

questions.q: Traditional network segmentation uses VLANs / firewalls between SUBNETS / ZONES. Microsegmentation goes finer: policy is enforced between INDIVIDUAL WORKLOADS based on identity / role / tags — even within the same subnet. A compromised VM cannot freely talk to its neighbours. Which describes microsegmentation?
choices: Creating many very small IP subnets
Placing every server behind its own physical firewall
Per-workload policy by identity/tag within a subnet
Encrypting all east-west traffic with IPsec
questions.explanation: Traditional segmentation: DMZ, VLAN zones. Micro-segmentation: policies between individual servers/workloads regardless of location. Prevents lateral movement after breach. SD-Access: SGT-based, ACI: EPG contracts, NSX: DFW.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A data centre needs Layer-2 reachability across racks AND beyond the 4094 VLAN limit. The team picks an L2-over-L3 overlay that encapsulates Ethernet frames in UDP (port 4789), uses a 24-bit VNI (~16M segments), and is routed by the underlay. Which?
questions.explanation: VXLAN solves VLAN scalability in data centers and SD-Access. Each VNI (VXLAN Network Identifier) is equivalent to a VLAN but allows 16M overlays. VXLAN EVPN uses BGP for control plane.

questions.q: Cisco ACI is a data-centre SDN solution with: APIC controller (HA cluster), spine-leaf physical fabric, INTENT-BASED policy via 'EPG' (Endpoint Group) + CONTRACTS, abstract / declarative model. Application teams define policies; the fabric implements them across physical + virtual workloads. Which describes ACI?
choices: A link-state routing protocol for spine-leaf underlays
Cisco ACI: DC SDN with APIC + EPG/contract policy
A campus wireless LAN controller architecture
questions.explanation: ACI: APIC controller + Nexus 9000 spine/leaf. Policy model: Tenant → Application Profile → EPG (Endpoint Group). Contracts define allowed communication between EPGs. Automates data center provisioning via REST API.

questions.q: Two VXLAN data-plane modes: (A) FLOOD-AND-LEARN — VTEPs discover MACs via BUM traffic flooded across the underlay multicast; no control plane awareness; scalability issues at large fabric. (B) MP-BGP EVPN — VTEPs advertise MAC + IP bindings in BGP control plane; no flooding required. Which mapping?
choices: Flood-and-learn = BUM flooding; EVPN = BGP control plane
Both modes require underlay IP multicast to learn endpoints
EVPN floods BUM traffic while flood-and-learn uses BGP
They are two names for the same control-plane mechanism
questions.explanation: VXLAN with EVPN (Type 2 routes: MAC/IP; Type 3: multicast/BUM) uses BGP to distribute endpoint info before packets arrive. Eliminates flood-and-learn scalability issues. Standard for modern data center fabrics.

questions.q: Cisco SD-WAN (Viptela) has FOUR architectural roles. (A) vManage = single-pane orchestration / GUI / API. (B) vSmart = control plane (overlay routes + policy enforcement). (C) vBond = onboarding / NAT-traversal helper. (D) WAN-edge routers = data plane. Which mapping is correct?
questions.explanation: SD-WAN control plane: vSmart distributes OMP (Overlay Management Protocol) routes and policies. vBond performs initial authentication and NAT traversal. vManage provides GUI management. Data plane uses IPsec overlays.

questions.q: DMVPN has THREE phases. (Phase 1) hub-to-spoke ONLY (spokes can't talk directly). (Phase 2) DYNAMIC spoke-to-spoke tunnels via NHRP — spoke A discovers B's NBMA address and builds a direct GRE tunnel; hub stays in the routing path. (Phase 3) NHRP summarisation + redirects so the data plane goes spoke-to-spoke immediately. Which describes the phases?
questions.explanation: DMVPN uses mGRE + NHRP + IPsec. Hub-spoke-spoke communication: spoke queries NHRP for other spoke's RLOC, builds direct tunnel. Phase 2: full spoke-to-spoke. Phase 3: adds NHRP redirect for scalability.

questions.q: In DMVPN Phase 2 / 3, a SPOKE wants to build a tunnel directly to ANOTHER spoke (skipping the hub). It needs to RESOLVE the other spoke's PUBLIC (NBMA / underlay) IP from the spoke's overlay tunnel IP. The hub maintains a dynamic mapping table; spokes query it on demand via a specific protocol. Which?
choices: A routing protocol that advertises spoke prefixes to the hub
NHRP: query the hub for a spoke's NBMA address
An IPsec key-exchange protocol used for tunnel setup
A QoS marking mechanism applied to tunnel traffic
questions.explanation: NHRP is the 'phone book' for DMVPN. Hubs are NHS (Next Hop Servers); spokes register their IP. When spoke A needs to reach spoke B, it queries NHS, gets B's NBMA address, and builds a direct IPsec/GRE tunnel. allows spoke routers to dynamically discover the physical IP (NBMA address) of other spokes through the hub, enabling direct spoke-to-spoke tunnels in DMVPN Phase 2/3.

questions.q: Cisco SD-Access overlay control plane separates a device's IDENTITY (its IPv4/IPv6 address as seen by apps) from its LOCATION (the routing locator — the fabric edge node attached to). The mapping is kept in a control-plane database. Endpoints can move between fabric edges without renumbering. Which protocol?
questions.explanation: In SD-Access, LISP provides the control plane. EIDs are IP/MAC addresses of endpoints; RLOCs are the tunnel endpoints (fabric edges). LISP Map-Server/Resolver manages the mapping database for endpoint mobility.

questions.q: Cisco SD-Access architecture has two distinct planes. (UNDERLAY) Traditional IP routing (typically IS-IS) between fabric nodes — provides L3 connectivity for the overlay tunnels. (OVERLAY) VXLAN tunnels carrying user traffic in segments / tenants; LISP as control plane for endpoint mobility. Which describes them?
choices: Underlay = VXLAN tunnels; overlay = the physical IP routing
Underlay = routed IP (IS-IS); overlay = VXLAN with LISP
Both planes run a single shared OSPF process
Overlay is the cabling and underlay is the user traffic
questions.explanation: SD-Access underlay: routed access using IS-IS + PIM. Fabric nodes build VXLAN tunnels over underlay. Overlay: each VN (Virtual Network) is a VRF, segmented via SGT policies. Control plane: LISP for endpoint location.
